message.content:
{
  "needed": true,
  "prompt": "Implementation instructions for backend only — add server-generated, non-empty request_id to the two specified error response types, correlate it with server logs, and ensure front-end can display it for feedback. Do not change code, message, or HTTP status codes; do not add request_id to success responses or to any other error responses; do not include credentials or any user-provided input inside request_id.

Scope decision (backend): implement generation, propagation, logging, API schema changes for exactly the two error response types referenced in the requirement (the two error response schemas currently used by the API contract). Do not change any other responses. If either of the two error response types is emitted from different code paths, ensure every emission path includes request_id as specified.

Concrete implementation steps:
1) Request ID format and generation
   - Generate request_id server-side only using a cryptographically secure random generator. Recommended formats (choose one):
     a) UUID v4 (RFC 4122) string (e.g. 36-character dashed string), or
     b) 128-bit hex or URL-safe base64 string from secure random bytes (e.g. 32 hex chars or 22 base64-url chars). 
   - Do not derive request_id from any user input, session token, credential, or other client-supplied values. The generator must only use server-side entropy.
   - Ensure the produced string is non-empty and conforms to the chosen format. Enforce a generation success check and fail-safe fallback (generate again) if an invalid/empty value would be produced.

2) Where to generate and attach
   - Generate request_id as early as possible in the HTTP request handling pipeline (for example, a server middleware/filter that runs before routing), to ensure availability for logging and error emission. If an error happens before middleware runs, ensure a catch-all generation path so the two error responses still include request_id.
   - Attach request_id to a request-scoped context object (request local storage, thread-local, or equivalent framework context) so all downstream code and loggers can access it.
   - Important: do not automatically add request_id into every HTTP response body. Only include it in the two specified error response payloads.

3) Logging and correlation
   - Include request_id in all structured logs for the request lifecycle. Integrate into the logging context (e.g., MDC, log context fields) so every log line emitted while handling the request contains request_id.
   - When an instance of either of the two error responses is emitted, ensure the server log entry for that error (stack trace, error details) contains the same request_id returned in the response.
   - Persist request_id with logs into whatever logging/observability backend you use (file, ELK, Cloud logging, etc.) so support can search by request_id to find full traces.

4) Response payload change (only for the two specified error types)
   - Add a top-level field named request_id (type: string, non-empty) to only the two existing error response JSON schemas. Make this field required in those two error response schemas.
   - Explicitly preserve existing fields exactly as currently defined: do not change or remove code, message, or HTTP status code values. The new field is additive for those error responses only.
   - Example (for implementers): if current error JSON is {"code": "X", "message": "..."}, new error JSON must be {"code": "X", "message": "...", "request_id": "<generated>"} for those two error types. Do not change the order or semantics of code/message/status code.
   - Do not add request_id to success responses or to any other error response types.

5) API contract and documentation updates
   - Update the API specification (OpenAPI/Swagger or equivalent) to add request_id as a required string property in the two specified error response schemas. Use an explicit description: "request_id: server-generated non-empty string; correlates to server logs; safe to show to users; contains no credentials or user input."
   - Do not change the status codes, nor code/message fields in the spec.
   - Add a short note in the API changelog documenting this additive change and that only the two error types include request_id.

6) Security and privacy constraints
   - Ensure request_id includes no credentials, tokens, passwords, or any user input. Do not derive request_id from user identifiers, payloads, or headers that may contain PII.
   - If logs contain other sensitive details, ensure access controls for logs remain enforced; request_id itself should not leak secrets.

7) Front-end considerations (backend responsibilities only)
   - Return request_id as described so front-end can display it. Ensure the JSON key is exactly request_id and the value is a non-empty string.
   - Do not add any readable explanation text — keep it as a data field in the error payload so front-end can localize/display as needed.

8) Error emission paths and early errors
   - Identify every code path that can return either of the two error response types (including exception handlers, validation layers, authorization filters, or early middleware). In each path, ensure a request_id exists and is inserted into the response payload before writing the response body.
   - For errors occurring before request context establishment, produce a request_id at error-time and still log and return it.

9) Tests and acceptance criteria (automated)
   - Unit tests: for each of the two error response types, assert that the response JSON contains a request_id field that is a non-empty string and matches the backend generation format.
   - Integration tests: trigger the two error responses via HTTP and verify the returned status code, code, and message are unchanged, and that request_id is present and non-empty. Also assert that success responses and other error responses do NOT include request_id.
   - Logging tests: when a given request yields one of the two error responses, assert that server logs for that request contain the same request_id and that the log entries are queryable by that request_id (or at least included in structured logging output captured during the test).
   - Negative tests: validate that request_id never contains substrings of typical user inputs from the request (e.g., request body fields, query parameters, auth tokens) — this can be a test that the request_id doesn’t match any of those values or that generation is independent.

10) Backwards compatibility and rollout notes
   - Adding a new field to only two error responses is additive, but it is a change to those error payload schemas. Coordinate deployment with frontend teams to ensure they can safely parse and display the new field. Document that code, message, and status codes are unchanged.
   - Deploy the middleware and logging changes first, then enable inclusion in the two error responses in a controlled release. Ensure monitoring for any client parsing errors after rollout.

11) Acceptance checklist (must pass before merge)
   - request_id is generated server-side using secure randomness, format documented.
   - request_id attached to request context and present in structured logs for all request logs.
   - Both targeted error response types include request_id as a required non-empty string in the JSON body.
   - No changes to code, message, or HTTP status codes for any responses.
   - Success responses and all other error types do NOT include request_id.
   - API spec updated and tests added and passing.
   - Tests ensure request_id never includes user-supplied input or credentials.

12) Implementation hints (do not construe as required code)
   - Use framework middleware for generation and context propagation (e.g., Express middleware, ASP.NET middleware, Spring filter, etc.).
   - Use logging context facilities (MDC/ThreadContext) to attach request_id to logs.
   - Use standard UUID libraries or crypto-secure random bytes for generation.

Deliverables to produce in the backend repo:
   - Code changes implementing request_id generation, propagation, insertion into the two error responses, and logging integration.
   - Updated API spec and changelog entries.
   - Unit and integration tests described above.
   - A short runbook note: how to use request_id to look up logs and what fields to search in the logging system.

Explicit preserved constraints reiterated (do not omit):
   - Preserve existing code, message fields, and HTTP status codes exactly — do not modify their values or semantics.
   - Only the two specified error response types gain the new required non-empty string request_id field. Success responses and all other error responses must not include request_id.
   - request_id must be generated by the backend, must not include any credentials or user-supplied input, and must be correlated with server logs so front-end-provided request_id can be used in feedback/support.

If any contract ambiguity remains about which two error types are in-scope, stop and request explicit names/identifiers of those two error responses before implementing; do not guess."
}
